content: Sesame, scientifically known as Sesamum indicum, is a flowering plant belonging to the genus Sesamum. Its exact natural origin remains uncertain, though numerous wild relatives are found in Africa, with fewer in India. The plant has become widely naturalized in tropical regions globally and is cultivated primarily for its edible seeds. The leaves of the sesame plant are simple, measuring up to 14 cm (5 inches) in length, with an entire margin. At the base of the plant, the leaves are broad and lanceolate, up to 5 cm (2 inches) wide, but they narrow to just 1 cm (0.5 inches) wide on the flowering stem. The flowers are tubular, ranging in color from white to purple, and measure 3 to 5 cm (1 to 2 inches) in length, with a four-lobed mouth. Origins Although most wild species of the genus Sesamum are native to sub-Saharan Africa, researchers Zohary and Hopf suggest that sesame was first domesticated in India. This hypothesis is supported by morphological and cytogenetic similarities between domesticated sesame and the South Indian native species S. indicum. Additionally, archaeological evidence indicates that sesame was cultivated in Harappa, in the Indus Valley, between 2250 and 1750 BCE. More recent findings of charred sesame seeds in Miri Qalat and Shahi Tump in Pakistan's Makran region further support this claim. The identification of sesame seeds in the tomb of Tutankhamun in ancient Egypt is considered plausible but requires further verification. Etymology The word sesame originates from the Latin sesamum, which was borrowed from the Greek sēsámon, meaning seed or fruit of the sesame plant. This, in turn, was derived from Semitic languages, such as Aramaic (shūmshĕmā) and Arabic (simsim), and ultimately from Late Babylonian (shawash-shammu) and Assyrian (shamash-shammū), meaning plant oil. In some Middle Eastern languages, sesame is referred to by names derived from Middle Persian kunjid, which has influenced terms in several Western languages, such as Russian (kunzhut), Estonian (kunžuut), and Yiddish (kunzhut). In Brazil, sesame is known as gergelim, while in Spanish, it is called ajonjolí. In Hindi, it is referred to as gingli. The Arabic noun jaljala, meaning sound or echo, is thought to describe the rattling sound of ripe seeds within the capsule. In the southern United States and the Caribbean, where sesame was introduced by African slaves, it is also known by its African name, benne. Mythological Background According to Assyrian legend, the gods drank wine made from sesame seeds when they met to create the world. In early Hindu mythology, sesame seeds symbolized immortality. In Urdu literature, sesame seeds are used in proverbs, such as til dharnay ki jagah na hona, meaning a place so crowded that there is no room for even a single sesame seed, and in tilon mein teil nahi, referring to a person who is very stingy, implying that there is no oil left in this sesame. Uses in Food and Cuisines Sesame is primarily cultivated for its oil-rich seeds, which vary in color from cream-white to charcoal-black. Lighter-colored seeds are generally more valued in Western and Middle Eastern cuisines, while black varieties are prized in East Asia. Sesame seeds are used whole in cooking for their rich, nutty flavor, though heating can damage their beneficial polyunsaturated fats. The seeds are also pressed to extract sesame oil. Sesame seeds are commonly added to breads, such as bagels and hamburger buns, and are baked into crackers, often in stick form. They are also sprinkled on sushi and incorporated into salads and baked snacks in Japan. Roasted tan and black sesame seeds are used to make the seasoning gomasio. In Greece, sesame seeds are used in cakes, while in Togo, they are a main ingredient in soups. In Sicily, sesame seeds are eaten on bread. In the United States, about one-third of the sesame crop imported from Mexico is purchased by McDonald's for their sesame seed buns. In Punjab, Pakistan, and Tamil Nadu, India, a sweet ball called Pinni (Urdu: پنی) or Ell urundai (Tamil) is made from sesame seeds mixed with sugar. In Tamil Nadu, a ground powder called Milakai Podi, made from sesame and dried chili, is used to enhance flavor and is consumed with traditional foods like idli. Ground sesame seeds are also used in sweet confections. Sesame seeds can be processed into a paste called tahini, which is used in dishes like hummus, and into a Middle Eastern confection called halvah. In India, the Middle East, and East Asia, sesame seeds are mixed with honey or syrup and roasted to make popular treats, such as pasteli in Greece. In Japanese cuisine, goma-dofu (胡麻豆腐) is made from sesame paste and starch. East Asian cuisines, such as Chinese and Vietnamese, use sesame seeds and oil in dishes like sesame seed balls (jin deui in Cantonese) and bánh rán. Sesame flavor, derived from oil or roasted seeds, is also prominent in Korean cuisine, where it is used to marinate meat and vegetables. Tempura chefs blend sesame and cottonseed oil for deep-frying. Sesame oil was the preferred cooking oil in India before the introduction of peanut oil. While sesame leaves are edible, recipes in Korean cuisine that call for sesame leaves often refer to perilla leaves due to mistranslation. Nutrition and Health Treatments Sesame seeds are rich in manganese, copper, and calcium, with unhulled seeds containing 90 mg of calcium per tablespoon and hulled seeds containing 10 mg. They also provide vitamin B1 (thiamine) and vitamin E (tocopherol). Sesame seeds contain lignans, including sesamin, which are phytoestrogens with antioxidant and anti-cancer properties. Among edible oils, sesame oil has the highest antioxidant content. Sesame seeds also contain phytosterols, which are associated with reduced blood cholesterol levels, but they do not contain caffeine. Grinding or pulverizing sesame seeds before consumption enhances nutrient absorption. In ancient Babylon, women consumed halvah, a mixture of honey and sesame seeds, to maintain youth and beauty, while Roman soldiers ate it for strength and energy. Despite their nutritional benefits, sesame seeds are a common allergen. Erroneous claims have suggested that sesame seeds contain THC, but this misunderstanding arises from the use of sesame oil as a delivery medium for the synthetic THC drug dronabinol. Sesame oil itself does not naturally contain THC. Sesame oil is used in traditional Indian Ayurvedic medicine for body massage and treatments, such as abhyanga and shirodhara. Ayurveda considers sesame oil the most viscous of plant oils and believes it can alleviate health issues associated with Vata dosha aggravation. Cultivation Sesame is cultivated on over 5 million acres (20,000 km²) worldwide. India is currently the largest producer, but the crop is also grown in China, Burma, Sudan, Mexico, and Ethiopia, among other countries. Commercial production in the United States reportedly began in the 1950s, but the U.S. imports more sesame than it grows. Pests Sesame plants serve as a food source for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, including the Turnip Moth.
